title: Form and Ellington's influence; Superman and Concerto for Cootie
summary: He wanted the pieces to hang together after Ellington.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: I think what was different there was the type of form. It was sort of an open ended thing where it closed at the end. I'm sure I was overwhelmed by Ellington's band at

that time, they way they got through their things; but I couldn't do that because I wasn't there. If I had been part of Ellington's band maybe, but those things are hung together in such a way. So having them hang together got to be very important and I guess the only way I could do it at that time was that way. Today it might be a little different, but it worked.
Frankly, I think it's--just to take an arbitrary example, "Superman" is just a good a piece and as ambitious a piece as "A Concerto for Cootie" that Duke wrote for Cootie, and works just as well.

Whether it's as valuable as a piece of art I don't know. Duke's certainly was; whether mine was, I don't know. It wasn't done for that reason, it was done just to do it. It worked out to be fine, but that piece is a little longer.
It was an LP; no, it wasn't an LP; what was it? Four and a half minutes.
It's sort of an scope or something where you try to make the whole thing hang together.
I think they all certainly did.
They did, for whatever it was; they did.
